Costs & payback

Solar payback periods, explained honestly

What payback really measures, which inputs move it most, and how to stress-test any payback figure before you trust it.

Published 22 July 2026Updated 15 October 20268 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

"Payback in four years" is the most repeated sentence in solar sales, and the most abused. Payback is a legitimate measure — how long it takes for accumulated savings to equal the net cost of the system — but it is only as honest as the assumptions fed into it. This article shows how the arithmetic works so you can audit anyone's version of it, including ours.

The basic arithmetic

Simple payback is net cost divided by annual savings. An illustration of the maths: a system costing $6,000 after incentives, saving $1,200 per year, pays back in about five years. Those figures demonstrate the calculation — they are not a price prediction for any household. The interesting part is never the division; it is what sits inside the two numbers.

What actually moves the number

  • Net cost after incentives — the STC discount and any state support reduce the amount that needs paying back. Confirm how the incentive is treated in the price rather than taking a discounted total on faith.
  • The price of the energy you displace — savings are mostly avoided imports, so they depend on your usage rate. A household paying a higher rate per kWh saves more from the same generation.
  • Self-consumption share — a kilowatt hour used at home avoids the full retail rate; the same hour exported earns the feed-in tariff, usually a fraction of it. The more of the generation the house uses, the shorter the payback.
  • Behaviour — schedulable loads (pool, hot water, EV, laundry) moved into daylight raise self-consumption without any hardware change.
  • Time — tariffs change, feed-in rates move, equipment degrades slightly, and electricity prices have historically risen more often than fallen. Any single-year figure is a snapshot of a moving system.
  • System size fit — generation far beyond consumption buys a longer payback, not a shorter one, because the surplus earns the low export rate.

Why your payback is not your neighbour's

Identical houses on the same street can post quite different paybacks. Roof orientations differ; one household is home in the day and one is not; one runs a pool pump at midday and the other overnight; the tariffs differ; one car is electric and charged in the sun, the next is petrol. Payback is a property of a household's behaviour and tariff as much as of its hardware — which is why template quotes that promise a single figure to a whole suburb should be read with suspicion.

Payback is not the whole story

  • Simple payback ignores everything after it. Panels keep generating for decades past the crossover point, and that back half of the life is where the returns become large.
  • It ignores the time value of money — $1,200 saved in year eight is worth less than $1,200 today. Financed systems need the loan's interest inside the arithmetic.
  • For batteries the shape differs: higher net cost, savings concentrated in the import–export price gap, and throughput limits that define the productive life. Battery payback deserves its own calculation, not a quiet assumption inside a panel quote.
  • Non-financial returns are real: outage resilience, price insulation, and not caring quite so much what the market does next.

How to stress-test any payback figure

  1. Ask for the assumptions in writing: usage rate, feed-in rate, self-consumption percentage, generation per kW, and incentive treatment.
  2. Check that savings are valued at the retail rate for self-consumed energy and the feed-in rate for exports — not the retail rate for everything.
  3. Confirm costs are net of incentives, and that the incentive assumption matches current official rules.
  4. Apply the pessimism pass: what happens if electricity prices stay flat, generation runs 10% low, and nobody shifts a single load? If the business case collapses under those, it was fragile.
  5. Update it with reality: after twelve months, your own bills and monitoring data replace every assumption. That calibrated figure is the only one worth relying on.

A payback figure is a model, not a promise

No honest estimate guarantees a payback period, because weather, prices and behaviour all influence the result. Demand ranges and assumptions; after the first year, insist on reality.

Key takeaways

  • Payback = net cost ÷ annual savings; both numbers deserve interrogation.
  • Self-consumption is the main lever — usage rate savings beat feed-in income many times over.
  • Payback is household-specific: tariff, behaviour and roof shape all move it.
  • Simple payback ignores the decades of generation after the crossover point.
  • Stress-test with pessimistic inputs, then recalibrate with a year of real data.
